utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case Number IT-99-36-T, The Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can hear you in a language that I can understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, appearances, Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. It's Joanna Korner, Julian Nicholls, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I thank you, and good morning to you all. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Aleksandar Vujic, and I am here together with David Cunningham and John Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you all. So what are these two CDs here?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are videos, a couple of the exhibits that I intend to use during the questioning of the expert witness in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I was just able to get them digitised a couple of days ago, and copied and given out to everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. With regard to that report, we've read it, all of us already. We've read the report of your expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, do I want to say with regard to those videos that I want to express my gratitude to the Office of the Prosecutor, and especially David Akerson for assisting in getting those on to CD-ROMs for me. I just want to make that a matter of the record. It was very kind of David to help me with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just deal first with the question that's just come up from Your Honour's query about these CDs. First, Your Honour, Mr. Ackerman said the Prosecution needed to file a motion as to whether they need to cross-examine Mr. Shoup. I see not the slightest need to clutter the Registry with more paper. I think it's already been made clear that we do wish to cross-examine Mr. Shoup. The second thing is this, I raised with Mr. Ackerman, Your Honours would have seen there's not a single document referred to in Mr. Shoup's report, actual exhibit in the case or any other document. He refers in the main to his own book. I raised with Mr. Ackerman, I think, after Court when we sat last week that I would like to have by Wednesday a list of the documents that Mr. Ackerman intended, if at all - he may not be intending to use any documents - that he was going to use with Mr. Shoup. I've spoken to Mr. Ackerman about this, and I'm now told I may be lucky if it's Monday. Your Honour, that, in my submission, will not do. As it is, we waived, and we are prepared to waive our right for a proper disclosure of the report in time to prepare. Even if Mr. Shoup is not here and Mr. Ackerman is not sure entirely which exhibits he will be using, nonetheless he must have a list of exhibits he intends to show Mr. Shoup, and I would ask that that be given to me today. I understand the witness will be arriving tomorrow. And at the very latest, Your Honour, if Mr. Ackerman declines to give us a list of documents he's going to show Mr. Shoup, then if on Friday I would like, before the holiday, a complete list of exhibits which are intended to be used with this witness, as I say, if any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Expert is arriving tomorrow, you said?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So Mr. Ackerman tells me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had a bit of a dispute with the powers that be at the Tribunal. I wanted him here earlier, and they refused to bring him earlier. So this is the best I can do. And that took quite a lot of persuasive talk. But I finally managed to get him here. Probably not quite enough time to spend as much time with him as I wanted to. I didn't make any trips to the United States and sit with him. I probably in retrospect maybe should have done that. I thought it would be a waste of money in some ways because I thought I could bring him here earlier, but I wasn't able to. I am not going to give the Prosecutor a list of documents that I'm going to show him because that would be a violation of the work product exception, I'm quite certain. I will immediately, as soon as I know, notify the Prosecutor of any documents that I'm going to use during his examination. Your Honour will remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's what she meant. No?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, it's not, Your Honour. The witness is going to start testifying on Tuesday. Monday is a holiday. I'll be here, but nonetheless I'd like the documents by -- the list by close of business -- in fact, before close of business on Friday so that we ourselves can assemble the documents, rather than coming to Court with I don't know how many volumes we've reached so far. Your Honour, in my submission, if we don't get it, it will lead to a delay because we will object to the witness starting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You mean the documents that Mr. Ackerman will be using if he will be using them in the course of his examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: His examination-in-chief. Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: From what I heard said, a violation of -- "I'm not going to give the Prosecutor a list of the documents that I'm going to show him because that would be a violation of the work product exception."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I've never heard anything so odd in all my life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. I just wanted to make it clear to myself whether I was understanding well or --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's what he's trying to say. In my submission that doesn't even begin to have merit as an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But Your Honour, I'm saying simply this: We have been understanding about proper summaries of witnesses being delivered to us the night before the witness testifies, the list of documents the same. But for an expert witness, Your Honour, for whom we have been given a weeks' notice before he's being called of what he's going to say, it is not in our submission in any way unfair or a breach of any sort of confidentiality -- there is no confidentiality between counsel and an expert to that extent. It's not like a client's instructions. But we are saying, Your Honour, that it would be right and proper for Your Honour to make an order that the proposed documents to be used with - even if not all of them to be used - proposed documents to be used with the expert are given to us by Friday at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the gentleman that's coming to testify was born ten years before I was. And I think it's very unlikely that on the day he arrives that it will be a very productive day because of the jet lag and so forth. He's 74 years old. The first, I think, real opportunity to start going through documents with him in the proofing process would be on Friday. I am not going to, unless I'm absolutely ordered to do that, provide Ms. Korner with a list of documents that I intend to show him during the proofing process. I would love to have gotten that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think that's what you were referring to, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It is. It's exactly what she is referring to. That's what she wants.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm trying to get some idea of the documents he will be using here. Clearly the documents that he's going to show the expert are the ones that he intends to use. He may in the end discard them. There may be a list given to us which contains more documents that are actually used. Quite often we have done the same, particularly for cross. But nonetheless I am asking for an indication from our point of view so we can know what areas because it's very unclear at the moment what this report I may say is designed for. Dr. Donia gets but one mention in the course of the whole report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact, that leads me again because I would have imagined something different.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's why we're trying to establish, which I say is very unclear from the report, to what areas this expert evidence is being called, and the documents that are going to be used may give us a clearer indication. An expert -- we're not supposed to stagger into Court totally unsure of where this is going, what this is about. So, Your Honour, that's what I'm asking for, and I'm asking Your Honour to make an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, while your discussing it, if you look -- if you check the record, you'll see numerous instances where Ms. Korner said I can't supply a list of documents because I haven't yet proofed the witness, and I said I agree, Your Honour, until she proofs the witness she can't supply the list. That's the same position I'm in. What's good for the goose is good for the gander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, we'll discuss it later and we'll let you know. Either through formal order or through the registry. Final solution would be that -- is it possible for you to be in contact on a Saturday, for example? Is it usual, or would it be...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's perfectly possible save for this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because then we can start on Wednesday, which will give you -- Monday is a holiday here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only thing I say about this weekend is there is an advocacy training course being run over the weekend which I'm involved, which is why I said I will be at work on Monday. But over Saturday and Sunday, it's going to be a bit difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the best solution would be we start on -- because I can quite understand if the gentleman who is coming over is in his 70s, I would -- in his 70s, 72, 73, something like that -- 74. I mean, I can't expect Mr. Ackerman, feeling ten years younger, to be able to run him over and come back on Friday with -- so I would rather say we start on Wednesday than Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not -- at the moment, I'm not asking for that. I'm with Your Honours on this at the moment, that we should keep the momentum going on this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. I agree, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm merely pointing out that if I only get the list of documents on Monday and it is an extensive list, then it may well that be I'll have to ask Your Honours for a delay while we sort out what this is all about, or alternatively ask for a delay between -- at the end of examination-in-chief and cross-examination, which is probably more sensible. Your Honour, but I do say this, it's not the same as a witness as to fact who has made a statement sometime ago. Mr. Ackerman has employed, as I understand, Mr. Shoup to do this report for a considerable period of time before today. And therefore, must have an idea of what it is that he wants the expert to deal with. But if Your Honours won't make that order, well, then, Your Honours, all I can say is that we may, as I say, be asking for a break between chief and cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm quite certain that by Friday afternoon, 3.30, 4.00, that I will have a list of documents. It won't be a complete list, but there will be a list. It could very well be a complete list by then, I don't know. I will give whatever I have to Ms. Korner on Friday. I'm not going to sit there until Monday and wait to give it to her. But what I'm saying I may not have everything by Friday. I just may not have time to do that by Friday. There may be a supplement that I would give her on Monday. But I think -- I don't know, but I would think 70, 80 per cent of what I'm going to use probably will be known by Friday afternoon. That's my guess, and that's what I will undertake to do. I have no interest whatsoever in not telling Ms. Korner the documents that I'm going to use just as some kind of a trick or something. When I know what they are, she'll know what they are. But until then, I can't -- you can enter all the orders you want, I can't give her anything I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No one suggested that, Mr. Ackerman. All right. So shall we take it that there is an undertaking on your part that you'll do your utmost so that you hand to Ms. Korner as complete a list as possible on Friday. And if that is not possible, you then continue either Saturday or Sunday or Monday, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour. And actually, the Netherlands Institute for War Documentation was cited extensively throughout his report, and Ms. Korner should assume that we're going to several parts of that report from that institute.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then I'd like copies, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What about the CIA?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Dr. Shoup says that it's not available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, there's volume 1, volume 2, and he alleges that volume 2 contradicts what is contained in volume 1, and we've only got bits and pieces of it. I am not in a position to know because I didn't want to ask before --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to wait and see with interest whether we were going to be given the unpublished manuscript by Mr. Hayden. But Your Honour, I think anything the Defence propose to use which is not in the public domain, such as Mr. Shoup's book, which we do have a copy of, we would like to be provided with copies with, and that, please, certainly by Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Netherlands Institute for War Documentation has a website in the footnotes to the report. That's where I've gotten it. You can get it from the same place. All you have to do is go to that website and you can print it out until you turn blue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's very nice. But actually, rather than have one of our staff print it out, we'd like a copy, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No. It's publicly available. I'm not going to spend my money to copy it and print it for you. It's publicly available; it's on the World Wide Web. Go get it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I take some slight umbrage at the tone in which that is said. Your Honour, it is the duty of the Defence as we did -- we've supplied, when we were using copies of Glas, we supplied them -- to supply us, please, with the documents which are not part of the exhibits in this case on which the expert intends to rely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we need to see them as well, because again I was not in a position to know, and obviously, I didn't want to ask until I first put the question to you which of the documents that -- main documents that report refers to are available or not. And particularly, I was interested in the CIA documents because if they were available to the expert, I don't see why they shouldn't be available to you or to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think he has got them. What I understood, he's quoting from a New York Times article about it. I don't know, but if he has got them then, of course, the Court and we should be supplied with them. Equally, if he has sight or a copy of an unpublished - he says in one of the footnotes - manuscript by Mr. Hayden which we don't have, we'd like that, too. So Your Honour, I'm going to say that Mr. Ackerman must supply us with those types of documents in the same way as we supplied him things that were going to be used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. What else? Mr. Donia. Mr. Donia, I had, of course, told you -- I had asked you actually whether you intended to bring him over, et cetera. I had not seen, obviously, Mr. Shoup's report at the time, and I was put on guard eventually when -- during the last sitting by Mr. Ackerman himself who said there would be very little reference, if any, to Mr. Donia's report. So as far as I am concerned at least, and I think my two colleagues also agree with me, I have no more feeling about it whether he should be here or not, it's up to you whether you require him here or not. In other words, I do not anticipate that there will be any questions necessary, needed from our part to Mr. Donia at this stage anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, like Your Honour I haven't had an opportunity to read the report. I think that's evident. I think there are two reference to Dr. Donia. Dr. Donia does have a number of professional commitments. So in those circumstances, we don't propose to bring him back here for the purposes of listening to Mr. Shoup.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only other question is Your Honours raised that you may wish to put more questions to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: BT --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: BT-94. Can Your Honours confirm that because we'll make arrangements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think you said you'd come back to us on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In that case, Your Honour, we'll make arrangements to have him brought over the week after next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Week after the next. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And the other person we checked, and you are right. He is a legal assistant to my surprise in one of the other cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: A number of people's surprise, I think, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we do require him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think Your Honours are making arrangements through the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think that actually changes anything as far as -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that's about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if we could get the heating turned down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please. I didn't say anything because I am not feeling well at all. I'm running a temperature, and so I thought it's me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, it's very hot in here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, usher, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I did ask beforehand, but obviously nobody has done anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, you could, because it is indeed hot, but I thought it was me. That's why I said I will at one moment I was going to tell you if you see me fainting, please bear with me because I did faint yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know Your Honours had a very long afternoon yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Or Your Honour did, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Also a long morning because we had an in camera meeting starting at 9.30, Judge Schomburg and Judge Mumba. That's why I couldn't continue a meeting with Judge Taya and Judge Janu. I had to stop. Today I have a meeting in the morning, a meeting at 1.45, Rules meeting, and then a sitting again in Deronjic until 7.00. The earlier I go home, the better because...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hope we won't detain Your Honour much longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I have seen --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I start really with the last aspect or the last person, and I think we need to go into private session, please, for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we would be prepared to restrict the application for the rebuttal witness to just the aspect of the property that Your Honours have talked about, Your Honour, no. We've considered the matter, and we say it's proper rebuttal, the other part of that evidence because what was led was evidence about 1993 and 1994 and Mr. Brdjanin's attitude, which we hadn't led, and that witness, we anticipate, will go into that period, so we had that evidence in respect of that period, but not in respect of 1992, that witness. Your Honours, our application will remain that we'd be able to call that witness on all aspects of her statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You didn't even mention this in your Prosecution motion to call evidence in rebuttal with regard to this witness. You just said regarding his contact and relation to the property --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I said right along that we never intended to do a written motion, that we did one at speed because we were asked to provide an indication that I wish to supplement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, all right. Okay. The position then, we hoped that you would have restricted this. We have discussed in camera the question with regard to the fourth witness. I think the position now is that we will hand down a short written decision in due course, the course of this week. It's the understanding that with regard to rebuttal of the evidence regarding the abbreviations, this is going to be supplemented by a redacted version and that your request to produce the letter from Novi Grad Municipality, you can make a statement. You can perhaps even -- you can even perhaps declare that it is based on a letter that you have received from Novi Grad Municipality --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to pursue the matter. It was there because it was a part of a number of things, but it's certainly not, in my submission, worthwhile pursuing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will later on hand down a decision this week. Don't expect a detailed decision, it's going to be a pretty straightforward decision, yes or no, obviously explaining why, but very short, very concisely. Regarding your -- I think we need to go into private session for a moment because it may be that this was a protected witness. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I've indicated to Mr. Ackerman is this report by the Netherlands Institute is enormous. I attempted -- the reason I said that Mr. Ackerman must provide copies is I attempted to print off from the Internet a very small part of that report, and it took forever. Which is why I said to Mr. Ackerman he must provide the report to us. In the adjournment, I've said to Mr. Ackerman, provided we are given the page numbers that he intends to use and the areas generally, then we'll do our own printing off the Internet for that report. Because, I mean, as Mr. Ackerman knows, it's very difficult. It take a long time. You have to keep going back to the next chapter. It's set out in chapters and so you can't just say -- and you don't want to print out the whole report because it's something like 800 pages, I think. If we're given the page numbers he's going to be referring to and the general areas, then we'll arrange our own printing. I will, however, say that we would ask for this unpublished manuscript of Mr. Hayden. There, we have no method of getting a hold of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is a big problem. I personally hate to take anything written for granted if it's only a part of a document or of a book or et cetera without having the opportunity at least to glance through and see for myself what I need to see. The other problem that we have, and I am -- I have been dealing with Madam Chuqing to sort it out, there seems to be only two copies of the book in our library, and they are both on loan. My idea was to take advantage of the fact that I am not feeling well, stay at home, and stay reading. And do you have spare copies that you can lend us --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, you'll recall a few days ago you suggested that you were going to take me up on my offer. I have -- they're on order. There are three of them coming here by DHL. They should probably arrive today. As soon as they arrive, I'll get them to Reinhold or Ken or somebody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Because Madam Chuqing offered to photocopy the books for the three of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's too much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a cumbersome job. I mean, if we can make use of the book, it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The only place I could get them was from the publisher in the US, and I think they were sending them DHL last week. So I think they will arrive today. I suggested that probably once you were finished with them, they would be donated to the Tribunal library or some such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I tell you why, Mr. Ackerman, because the report of your witness starts precisely with a very straightforward declaration. First of all, it refers throughout as you go along to the book. And he is making his report in the plural sometimes, and then he jumps into the personal, singular sometimes. And he makes a very fundamental declaration in the beginning saying that he, out of the two authors, he is the one who believes that the Serbs were demonised and so on and so forth. I know I wouldn't like to go any further than this for the time being. And then in a substantial part of his report, he tries to explain why, according to him, we should agree with his approach, with his belief. Now, I personally wouldn't even dream of proceeding to decide in my mind on whether he is right to come to that conclusion without having had the opportunity of reading the book, which obviously is -- covers much broader area of the events and of some of the considerations. For example, there is almost nothing in the report about the establishment of Republika Srpska almost. It is conspicuously absent from the report. And I wish to read the book in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've said more than once, I think, that the book is part of his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you'll see in his report that by reference he makes it part of his report. I didn't see any -- nor did he see any reason to just rewrite portions of that book just to make his report bigger. So you're correct, you really should have it. It's part of what he's doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the right approach. But again, he draws conclusions which one presumably ought to find in the book. But the reasons behind those conclusions are not contained in the report, but they are contained in the book. I would assume so, you know. And the other problem that I have is he bases a lot on the CIA --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I happened to think that he's wrong, that it hadn't been published. I'm going to make some inquiries, and I think we maybe able to -- unless he's going to provide it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It has been published, Ms. Korner, I think from what I have read in the report itself that it's definitely worth going through reading because it's a political -- very detailed political assessment, seemingly based on information on the ground. And the thing is that if it was available in one way or another to the author or to the expert, and it is not made available to us, it's not a question of control only; it's a question of trying to understand --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As I understand his report, Your Honour, he's relying on secondary sources there, a report in the New York Times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I also take it that the CIA reports --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm making inquiries at the moment, but I have reason to believe it may have been published.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll tell you my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My understanding is that the first -- there are two CIA reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My understanding is that the first one is not available. The second one clearly is publicly available. It costs 275 dollars. I've already got it on order. And it's coming DHL, and it should arrive today or tomorrow. But it's huge. It's called "Balkan Battlefields" or something like that. That's the name of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what it was called. So was the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That one has been published not just by the CIA, but by some person who apparently was its author on behalf of the CIA, so it's privately published also. I found it on Amazon.com and was able to order it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My whole point rests on two consideration: Number one is that if reference is made to the reports, and they are available, they should be made available. That's number one. Because there is reference to these reports on several parts of your expert's report. That's number one. Secondly, is that according to the expert, in certain parts or with regard to certain aspects, the second report contradicts the first in certain basic considerations, basic conclusions. Are you telling me that the second one may be available or is available, but the first one is not? That would pose a problem. Perhaps if you can reach Mr. Shoup before he leaves or if he has left already, if he can bring with him whatever is available from that first report, provided it can be made available to us. I don't know. But it would solve some problems for us because I don't fancy reading a report which makes reference to several other reports, documents, et cetera, and then take everything for granted, you know. It's like when I'm examining students for their Ph.D. dissertation, you get references, and cross-references, fully aware that probably 50 or 60 per cent of the texts and the authors they refer to in their dissertation have never been consulted. But anyway... I would like as much information as possible because as Ms. Korner said, the report comes unaccompanied with any documents. It's only references to various documents. All right. Let's call it a day because I don't want to disappoint Judge Orie.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: One more thing. Can we go into private session.

procedural_notes.text: [The Trial Chamber and legal officer confer]
